source.title: L0 is not a neutral hyperparameter

record.tranche_reason: The post reports experiments on how SAE sparsity affects recovery of correlated toy features, but does not test dictionary-size splitting, parent-child input partitioning, or the specific splitting behavior named in any claim version.
record.gate_note: The experiments vary L0 while holding SAE width fixed at 20; they do not measure dictionary-size splitting. The reported results concern broken mixtures, feature hedging, and recovery of toy-model features, so they are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The post sweeps BatchTopK L0 at a fixed width of 20 in a correlated toy model and reports feature hedging and degenerate latents. It never varies dictionary size, so no splitting is measured. It also deliberately suppresses absorption by adding magnitude variance. Its Matryoshka-like multi-L0 loss targets hedging, not splitting. None of its results bear on V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also argue that a 'correct' L0 exists and should be sought, and frame the low-L0 failure as feature hedging.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic correlated-feature toy model and sweeps BatchTopK L0 at fixed width; it does not compare dictionary sizes or test the original splitting measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with SAE k relative to the toy model's approximate true L0; the mixed-loss outcome changes with lambda.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed width 20, k below the true L0 of about 5 mixes f0 into other latents (hedging), and MSE improves (0.42 vs 0.53 for the truncated correct SAE). k above 5 yields increasingly broken, degenerate latents without hedging.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In correlated toy data, an SAE L0 set below the true L0 incentivises feature hedging; an L0 set above it permits degenerate solutions.

fits_no_version.finding: A summed loss at k1=4 and k2=8 recovers the true features at λ=20; at λ=1 it still shows hedging.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A multi-L0 loss can recover true toy features when the true L0 is unknown, depending on the loss weighting.

record.problems: Evidence is from a single synthetic toy model with 20 features and fixed SAE width; results are described qualitatively, with no uncertainty estimates reported.

untested.parts: No change in dictionary size; width fixed at 20.
No large models or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families or concept hierarchy measured.
Absorption deliberately prevented via magnitude stddev; no parent/child firing measured.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes.
The multi-L0 objective is tested only against hedging and degenerate latents, not against splitting. Matryoshka SAEs are not trained.

record.verdict_notes: The comments mention that SAEs wider than the number of true features invent combination or duplicate latents. That result comes from an earlier post and was not run here, so it should not become a row. In this toy setup, splitting and absorption are out of scope by design.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of dictionary size or measurement of a smaller feature being replaced by finer features that partition its inputs and lie near its direction.
No large models or open SAE releases are tested for splitting.
No nested feature families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy are measured.
No parent-child latent firing or absorption behavior is measured, and no change to SAE size or sparsity is tested as a fix for absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or assessment of novel latents across dictionary sizes.
The study examines L0-related feature hedging in a toy model, but does not test whether splitting is an artifact of the objective or compare Matryoshka SAEs against splitting.

rows.subject: toy model (20 mutually-orthogonal true features)
rows.operation_detail: Train Global BatchTopK SAE with k=5, matching the toy model's approximate true L0.
rows.value: The SAE perfectly learns the true features.
rows.locator: Case 1: SAE L0 = Toy Model L0

rows.operation_detail: Train Global BatchTopK SAE with k=4, below the toy model's approximate true L0.

rows.value: The SAE merges f0 into all other latents rather than representing f0 directly; high-frequency latents appear more broken than lower-frequency ones.
rows.locator: Case 2: SAE L0 < Toy Model L0
rows.note: Qualitative result; the post calls this feature hedging.

rows.operation_detail: Train Global BatchTopK SAE with k=3, below the toy model's approximate true L0.

rows.note: The post describes the result as better than its Case 1 SAE, but still showing hedging.
rows.check: The note says the result looks better than the 'Case 1' SAE. That is the text's wording, but the comparison is presumably to the broken Case 2 (k=4) SAE, since Case 1 was perfect. Treat it as a reference to the hedging SAE.

rows.subject: toy model (20 mutually-orthogonal true features)
rows.operation_detail: Train with summed losses using k1=4 and k2=8, with lambda=20.
rows.measure: Recovery of underlying features and hedging
rows.baseline: k1=4, k2=8, lambda=1: dedicated f0 latent but clear hedging
rows.value: The true features are perfectly recovered.
rows.locator: Mixing high and low L0 penalties together
rows.note: The author says the low-L0 loss limits degenerate solutions while the high-L0 loss limits hedging.
rows.check: This row reports the study's own proposed multi-L0 method. It is fine as a related finding but bears on no version: it reduces hedging, not splitting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
